title: Optimising physiological birth and the birth environment
blurb: Create an environment and give the one-to-one, low-intervention care that supports physiological labour, including position, hydration and bladder care.
question: Ffion, 5 cm in her second labour at an alongside midwifery unit, arrives with her partner and sister. She is well and labour is progressing. What can the midwife do to support a physiological birth, and which interventions should she avoid?

teach.h: Supporting the body to do its work
teach.body: Formally: NICE NG235 asks for a culture of respect in every birth setting, one-to-one midwifery care, freedom to move and choose positions, support from birth companions, and no clinical intervention when labour is progressing with no concerns. In plain English: a calm, private, well-supported woman who can move, eat lightly, drink to thirst and empty her bladder labours well. The midwife's skill is knowing when to watch and when to act.

teach.caption: NICE NG235 1.3.3. Women may choose any setting and should be supported in that choice.

items: Greet her and her companions with a smile, introduce yourself and your role; ask what she wants to be called.
Respect personal space, privacy and dignity: knock and wait before entering.
Discuss her preferences and birth plan; make sure she knows her pain relief options.
Encourage her to adapt the environment to meet her needs.
Explain every procedure or observation before it happens and ask consent.
Show her how to summon help; say when you will return if you leave.
Hand over care in the room, with the woman at the centre.

teach.body: Do not offer intervention if labour is progressing with no concerns and the woman and baby are well. Do not perform routine amniotomy, or combine early amniotomy with oxytocin. Do not routinely use a numerical pain score. A vaginal examination should add important information; she can decline it or ask to stop at any stage. Review bladder care at least every 4 hours and offer a catheter if she cannot pass urine.

The midwife welcomes Ffion, her partner and sister, asks what she would like to be called and reviews her birth plan. She encourages her to adjust the lighting, music and furniture, to move freely and to avoid lying flat. Ffion drinks when thirsty and eats a light snack. The midwife stays with her, explains each observation before doing it, checks her bladder 4-hourly and does not offer amniotomy because labour is progressing well.

teach.text: More fluid is not better: drinking more than normal can cause hyponatraemia, with maternal and neonatal seizures. And ketones in the urine of a woman without diabetes are not treated with fluids.

items: One-to-one care; do not leave her alone except briefly or at her request.
Birth companions of her choice; encourage her to adapt the environment.
Any comfortable position except lying flat on her back.
Drink to thirst, light diet unless opioids or caesarean risk factors.
Positive balance 1,500 mL or hyponatraemia signs: obstetric review and sodium test.
No intervention, routine amniotomy or numerical pain scores when labour is progressing well.

summary: You can now create a respectful, private birth environment, provide one-to-one care and support movement, positions, eating and drinking. You can also recognise the risks of overhydration, keep bladder care on track and avoid unnecessary interventions when labour is progressing well.

A.q: Which positions should the midwife encourage during Ffion's first stage of labour?
options: Semi-recumbent on the bed for monitoring
Left lateral throughout the first stage
Any comfortable position except lying flat
Upright, with her feet supported in stirrups
A.why: NG235 1.4.12: encourage and help the woman to move and adopt whatever positions she finds most comfortable, except lying flat on her back.

whyNot.0: Restricting her to the bed for monitoring is not needed in low-risk labour.
whyNot.1: No single position is mandated in the first stage.
whyNot.3: Stirrups are not a recommended position for physiological labour.

A.q: What drinking advice should be given to a woman in established labour?
options: Drink when thirsty; isotonic drinks may help
Drink at least 1 litre of water each hour
Take small sips of water and no other drinks
Stop drinking once labour is established
A.why: NG235 1.8.17: drink during labour when thirsty; isotonic drinks may be more beneficial than water; there is no benefit to drinking more than normal.

whyNot.2: Isotonic drinks may be more beneficial than water.
whyNot.3: Women should drink when thirsty in labour.

A.q: What does NICE NG235 say about leaving a woman alone in established labour?
options: Check on her in the room every 30 minutes
Do not leave her except briefly or at her request
Join her once she reaches full dilatation
Leave her with her companion between the checks
A.why: NG235 1.4.6: do not leave a woman in established labour on her own except for short periods or at her request.

whyNot.0: Intermittent checks are not one-to-one care.
whyNot.2: One-to-one care is needed throughout established labour.
whyNot.3: A companion does not replace one-to-one midwifery care.

B.q: Kemi is in established labour. She has had no opioids and has no risk factors for caesarean birth. She asks for some toast. What should the midwife say?
options: Clear fluids until the baby is born
Nil by mouth once labour is established
Food after an anaesthetist review
A light diet is fine if she wishes
B.why: NG235 1.8.18: she can eat a light diet in established labour if she wishes, unless she has received opioids or develops risk factors for caesarean birth.

whyNot.0: Restricting her to clear fluids is not recommended.
whyNot.1: Nil by mouth is not recommended for low-risk labour.
whyNot.2: An anaesthetist review is not needed for a light diet.

B.q: Lou, who does not have diabetes, has ketones on urinalysis in labour. She is drinking to thirst and is otherwise well. What should the midwife do?
options: Start intravenous fluids to clear the ketones
Avoid treating the ketonuria with fluids
Ask her to drink an extra litre of water
Transfer her for intravenous dextrose
B.why: NG235 1.8.29: do not routinely advise oral fluids or give IV fluids to treat ketonuria in women who are not diabetic.

whyNot.0: IV fluids are not given routinely for ketonuria.
whyNot.3: Ketonuria alone is not a reason for transfer or dextrose.

B.q: Mia is expecting her second baby and her pregnancy is low risk. She asks how planned home birth compares with an obstetric unit. What should the midwife tell her?
options: Home: fewer interventions and no difference for the baby
Obstetric unit: fewer interventions for her
Home: a small increase in adverse outcome for the baby
Home: more interventions than an obstetric unit
B.why: NG235 1.3.3: for low-risk multiparous women, home or midwifery unit birth is associated with a lower rate of interventions and no difference in outcome for the baby.

whyNot.1: Intervention rates are higher in obstetric units.
whyNot.2: The small increase in adverse outcome applies to nulliparous women planning home birth.
whyNot.3: Home birth is associated with fewer interventions.

C.q: At a midwifery unit, Erin has drunk large volumes and her fluid balance is positive by 1,700 mL. She now has a headache and seems confused. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Encourage isotonic drinks instead of water
Start IV fluids to dilute her ketones
Obstetric review, sodium test and transfer
Reassess her fluid balance in 4 hours
C.why: NG235 1.8.28: with positive balance of 1,500 mL or more or signs of hyponatraemia, explain, request obstetric review, offer a sodium test and transfer from a midwifery-led setting.

whyNot.0: More fluid of any kind worsens hyponatraemia.
whyNot.1: IV fluids would worsen the problem.
whyNot.3: Symptoms suggest hyponatraemia now; waiting is unsafe.

C.q: Ella's midwife is finishing her shift. How should handover of care take place?
options: At the desk, to protect her privacy
By phone to the incoming midwife
Using the ward board and notes
In the room, with Ella at the centre
C.why: NG235 1.4.11: involve the woman in any handover of care, in the room when appropriate, with the woman at the centre of the discussion.

whyNot.0: Handing over away from her excludes her from decisions about her care.
whyNot.2: Written records support but do not replace an inclusive handover.

C.q: Which event is a midwifery staffing red flag under NICE NG4?
options: Triage completed within 15 minutes of her arrival
No midwife free to give 1:1 care in established labour
Pain relief given 20 minutes after she asks for it
A woman's companion leaving the room for a short break
C.why: NICE NG4 Box 3: any occasion when one midwife cannot provide continuous one-to-one care to a woman in established labour is a red flag; the midwife in charge decides how to respond.

whyNot.0: The red flag is a triage delay of 30 minutes or more.
whyNot.2: The red flag is a pain relief delay of more than 30 minutes.
whyNot.3: A companion taking a break is not a staffing red flag.

reteach.title: Calm, close, free
reteach.question: Think of three words for the conditions that help labour work: calm, close and free. What does each mean in practice?

blocks.body: Calm: a private, respectful room she can adapt, with procedures explained and consented. Close: a midwife who stays with her and the companions she chooses. Free: free to move, to change position, to drink when thirsty and eat lightly. Interventions come only when the clinical picture asks for them.

explain.body: Encourage the woman to adapt the environment to her needs, respect her privacy and dignity (knock and wait), support the companions she chooses and music of her choice.

test.q: How should the midwife approach the birth room environment?
options: Encourage her to adapt it to her needs
Keep the lights bright for observation
Ask companions to wait outside
Keep the door open for staff access
test.why: NG235 1.4.11: encourage the woman to adapt the environment to meet her individual needs, and respect her privacy and dignity.

whyNot.1: The woman, not staff convenience, should shape the environment.
whyNot.2: NG235 encourages support from birth companions of her choice (1.4.13).
whyNot.3: An open door compromises privacy and dignity.

explain.body: Be sure a VE is necessary and adds important information, explain why, ensure consent, privacy and comfort, and advise that she can decline before it starts or ask to stop at any stage.

test.q: What should Hana be told before a vaginal examination in labour?
options: Once begun, it must be completed
Her earlier consent covers all VEs
Her partner can consent for her
She can decline it or ask to stop
test.why: NG235 1.8.9: advise the woman that she can decline the examination before it starts, or ask to stop at any stage.

whyNot.0: She can withdraw consent at any stage.
whyNot.1: Consent is sought for each examination.
whyNot.2: A competent woman consents for herself.

explain.body: Review bladder care at least every 4 hours: frequency of passing urine and bladder sensation, fluid balance if sensation is abnormal, she cannot pass urine or she has IV fluids, and offer a catheter if there are concerns.

test.q: How often should bladder care be reviewed for a woman in labour?
options: Every hour throughout
Every 8 hours
At least every 4 hours
Once, on admission to the unit
test.why: NG235 1.8.25: review bladder care for women at least every 4 hours.

whyNot.0: Hourly is not the NG235 standard for bladder review.
whyNot.3: A single check misses later retention.

explain.body: If labour is progressing with no complications and the woman and baby are well, do not offer or advise clinical intervention. Do not perform routine amniotomy, or routine early amniotomy with oxytocin.

test.q: Rosa is progressing well in labour with intact membranes. What does NICE NG235 say about amniotomy?
options: Offer it routinely at 6 cm
Do not perform it routinely
Combine it with early oxytocin
Perform it to apply a scalp electrode
test.why: NG235 1.8.39: do not routinely perform amniotomy if labour is progressing with no complications or concerns.

whyNot.2: Do not routinely combine early amniotomy with oxytocin (1.8.40).
whyNot.3: There is no indication for a scalp electrode in uncomplicated labour.
